entry.title: Evening — Nov 22, 2026
entry.content:
PulseBrief's Evening Pulse


Sun, Nov 22, 13:00 → Sun, Nov 22, 18:00


Cyber Security


Cleverbridge warns hackers stole credit card numbers and CVVs


Nov 22, 16:43


E-commerce platform Cleverbridge says attackers breached its systems and stole customers' payment card data, including card numbers and CVV security codes. The summary does not say how many people are affected, how the attackers got in, or when the breach happened. The warning comes from the company itself.


Card numbers plus CVVs can be used for fraud right away, so anyone who bought software or services through Cleverbridge-powered checkouts should watch their statements and expect reissued cards.


Sources: BleepingComputer


Cyprus expels two Russian diplomats on suspicion of espionage


Nov 22, 16:56


Cyprus expelled two men suspected of working for Russian intelligence under diplomatic cover, Politico EU reports. The summary gives no detail on what they were accused of doing or on any Russian response.


This is a state-espionage story, not a cyber incident, but it shows continuing intelligence pressure on EU states. It is included because few cyber stories are in this window.


Sources: Politico EU


AI & Machine Learning


Signal moves to block Siri and Gemini from capturing chats on iOS and Android


Nov 22, 16:15


Signal announced new protections that block screenshots on iOS 27 and stop AI assistants from capturing conversations on supported Android devices. The summary does not say when the changes ship or which Android devices are covered. This is a first-party announcement from Signal, relayed by BleepingComputer.


OS-level AI assistants that can read the screen are now a confidentiality risk for private messaging, and this is a concrete response from a major secure messenger.


Sources: BleepingComputer


NYT Magazine: researchers race to build a mathematical safeguard to keep AI under human control


Nov 22, 13:27


The NYT profiles Mike Winer and his colleagues, who are trying to build a mathematical safeguard that keeps AI under human control. They fear they are running out of time. This is a long feature, not a new technical result, and the summary gives no details of the method.


It shows that AI-control concerns are reaching mainstream audiences, but it does not report a new capability or product.


Sources: NYT Business


The Verge: vibe-coding is spreading to hardware, with LLMs making gadget hacking easy


Nov 22, 14:00


The Verge's Stepback newsletter says people worldwide are now using LLMs to hack, mod and tweak their TVs, cameras and other devices. Hobbyists have always done this, but LLMs lower the skill barrier sharply. This is analysis, not new reporting.


If device modification gets this easy, expect more unofficial firmware and customized devices, which can bring both innovation and new security and support risks.


Sources: The Verge


Technology


Backblaze customers worry about personal data sale or sharing after a policy update


Nov 22, 16:16


Neowin reports that Backblaze customers are concerned that an updated policy allows their personal data to be sold or shared. The Hacker News thread has 115 points and 50 comments. The summary does not give the policy wording or any response from Backblaze.


Backblaze holds backups of personal and business data, so any loosening of its data-use terms is worth checking if you use it.


Sources: Neowin · Hacker News


As cars go digital, US consumers pay an extra $12 billion a year for repairs


Nov 22, 17:08


The Register reports that today's vehicles need software tools for repairs, and that subscriptions for those tools inflate insurance costs. The estimated added cost to US consumers is $12 billion a year. The summary does not say who produced the estimate.


It shows how software lock-in raises costs in physical goods, which adds to the right-to-repair debate.


Sources: The Register


C++26 is done (again): Herb Sutter's trip report from the November ISO meeting


Nov 22, 16:59


Herb Sutter's report from the November 2026 ISO C++ standards meeting in Búzios, Brazil says C++26 is done. The Hacker News thread has 32 points and no comments yet. The summary does not list the contents or the next steps.


A finished standard sets the schedule for compiler support and for what C++ teams can adopt.


Sources: Herb Sutter · Hacker News


Open Social Web Alliance launches and draws a lively Hacker News debate


Nov 22, 16:24


The Open Social Web Alliance site has drawn 183 points and 184 comments on Hacker News. The summary does not say who the members are or what the alliance plans to do.


It is an early signal about how decentralized social platforms might organize, and the heavy discussion suggests developer interest.


Sources: Open Social Web Alliance · Hacker News


Business & Markets


Protesters storm Meta offices in India over restored accounts and alleged bias


Nov 22, 16:15


Members of India's opposition Congress party youth wing protested at Meta's Delhi offices on Friday and appear to have entered the building, based on video shared by CNN. They want the accounts of party leaders restored. Two accounts were restored Friday, but a party official told Reuters that thousands more are affected, and the party warned of more protests. Congress accuses Meta of favoring Modi's BJP.


India is one of Meta's largest markets, and escalating political pressure over moderation raises regulatory and reputational risk there.


Sources: The Verge


COP31 climate talks collapse over fossil fuel disputes


Nov 22, 14:00


Climate leaders failed to reach a deal at COP31 despite warnings about runaway warming, with the sticking point being disagreement over fossil fuels. Politico EU covered the collapse in both English and French. The summary gives no detail on which countries blocked an agreement.


No deal means continued uncertainty for energy and climate policy, which affects investment planning across energy-intensive sectors, including data centers.


Sources: Politico EU · Politico EU (French)


NYC Mayor Mamdani at DealBook: Trump, Wall Street and wealth taxes


Nov 22, 14:00


New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani spoke with Andrew Ross Sorkin at the DealBook Summit about Trump, Wall Street and wealth taxes. The summary does not include what he said.


The mayor's stance toward Wall Street and taxes bears on business conditions in a major financial center, so read the full interview for specifics.


Sources: NYT Business


Global left rallies in Paris to make the case for taxing billionaires


Nov 22, 17:21


Politicians from Europe and the US gathered at economist Gabriel Zucman's summit to argue for taxing the super-rich. Politico EU notes that few of the attendees are in a position to act. The summary gives no specific proposals.


Wealth-tax proposals are gaining visibility on both sides of the Atlantic, but political power to pass them is limited for now.


Sources: Politico EU

entry.title: Afternoon — Nov 22, 2026
entry.content:
PulseBrief's Afternoon Pulse


Sun, Nov 22, 07:00 → Sun, Nov 22, 13:00


AI & Machine Learning


Major US banks ban third-party AI agents from logging into customer accounts


Nov 22, 12:00


Wired reports that major US financial institutions are barring third-party bots from logging into customer accounts. They are also warning that customers bear the cost of any bot mistakes. The summary names no specific banks and gives no effective dates.


It is an early sign that the financial sector will refuse agent access and push liability onto users, which affects any plan to let agents act on accounts.


Sources: Wired


Technology


Breakdown projects Anthropic's data center power at 87% gas and 11% coal by 2028


Nov 22, 09:57


A Better Data Center Project analysis of how AI is powered, covering bring-your-own-power and grid supply, drew 576 points and 644 comments on Hacker News. The thread title says 87% of Anthropic's power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028. The figures come from the project's own analysis, and the summary does not show the underlying methodology.


The heavy discussion shows that the energy source behind AI compute has become a public issue, which could bring scrutiny and regulation.


Sources: Better Data Center Project · Hacker News


Muru: an AI-assisted Rust server for Python apps, from the creator of mod_WSGI


Nov 22, 10:57


Simon Willison highlights Muru, a Rust-based server for Python web applications built with AI assistance by the creator of mod_WSGI. The Hacker News thread has 53 points and 8 comments. The summary gives no benchmarks or maturity details.


It is a credible author applying AI-assisted development to core web infrastructure, so it is worth a look if you run Python apps in production.


Sources: Simon Willison · Hacker News


Passive 'ghost' radar detects airborne threats using TV and mobile signals


Nov 22, 10:15


The Register describes a passive radar that piggybacks on existing TV and mobile signals to detect airborne threats without revealing its own position. The kit is compact enough to fit in an SUV. The summary gives no range or performance figures.


A radar that emits no signal is hard to locate or jam, which is a notable shift in defense sensing technology.


Sources: The Register


Business & Markets


Procter & Gamble to add more factory shifts that run without humans


Nov 22, 11:02


NYT reports that P&G, maker of Pampers and Bounty, operates 15 sites capable of running shifts unattended. It plans to add more in 2027 to cut costs. The summary gives no savings estimate or workforce impact.


A large consumer goods maker expanding lights-out manufacturing signals where automation spending and labor effects are heading.


Sources: NYT Business


All flights to and from Brussels and Charleroi airports canceled Monday amid strike


Nov 22, 11:30


Air traffic controllers will join a nationwide Belgian protest against government spending cuts. Politico EU reports that all flights to and from Brussels and Charleroi airports are canceled on Monday. The summary does not say how long the disruption will last.


Brussels is a hub for EU institutions and business travel, so expect rerouted trips and delayed freight on Monday.


Sources: Politico EU


Agriculture Secretary calls US cattle supply safe as screwworm cases rise


Nov 22, 11:01


NYT reports that officials say heavy rains in the Southwest have led to more screwworm cases in animals. They say mitigation efforts are working well. The summary gives no case counts or supply figures.


Rising animal infections alongside official reassurance is a risk to watch for beef supply and prices.


Sources: NYT Business

entry.title: Morning — Nov 22, 2026
entry.content:
PulseBrief's Morning Pulse


Sat, Nov 21, 18:00 → Sun, Nov 22, 07:00


Cyber Security


Microsoft discloses Entra Connect Health breach: attackers pulled admin emails and tenant configuration data


Nov 21, 19:01


Microsoft warned customers that attackers exploited a flaw in its Entra Connect Health service to read administrator and technical contact email addresses and tenant configuration data. A customer notice shared on Reddit describes read-only access to those records, not access to inboxes or messages. Microsoft fixed the cloud-side flaw on November 19. The details come from Microsoft's own notice, and the number of affected tenants has not been given.


Admin contact emails and tenant configuration data are useful for targeted phishing and reconnaissance against identity infrastructure, so expect follow-on social engineering aimed at your admins.


Sources: BleepingComputer · Cybersecurity News


FBI NCIC hack confirmed by Trump as USDA is also reported breached


Nov 21, 18:42


The FBI breach of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which law enforcement uses to share warrants and missing-persons data, was confirmed by President Trump in a Fox News interview. He called it 'not good'. CNN notes this is the second attack on the agency in recent months. Separately, NBC first reported a hack of the US Department of Agriculture, and Reuters reports that a payments database is the known extent so far, with former officials warning there may be more. The attacker and the data taken have not been disclosed.


This moves the FBI story from an unconfirmed report to an acknowledged incident, and the USDA intrusion suggests a wider campaign against federal systems.


Sources: The Verge · TechCrunch · SecurityWeek


Rackspace Spot breached via stolen credentials; attackers reached customer Kubernetes secrets


Nov 21, 23:59


Rackspace told customers that hackers used compromised credentials to get into its Rackspace Spot cloud platform. They deployed unauthorized workloads and accessed Kubernetes secrets in customer clusters. The warning is Rackspace's own notice to customers. The number of affected customers and the source of the credentials have not been given.


Exposed cluster secrets can hand attackers keys to databases, registries and other cloud services, so Spot customers should rotate every secret in the clusters at once.


Sources: BleepingComputer


Upload2Shell: patched Ghostscript flaw gives remote code execution through ordinary file uploads (vendor research)


Nov 21, 19:29


Security firm pwn.ai showed that a crafted file can escape Ghostscript's sandbox and run commands on the server that processes it. The flaw is CVE-2026-125396 and affects Ghostscript releases before 10.08.0. The researchers demonstrated it against WordPress, Roundcube webmail and Linux print servers. Applications often invoke Ghostscript indirectly to convert uploaded PDFs, PostScript and images. A fix is available, and no exploitation in the wild has been reported.


Ghostscript is buried inside many upload-handling pipelines, so you may be exposed without knowing it. Check server images and containers for versions before 10.08.0.


Sources: The Hacker News · Cybersecurity News · pwn.ai (vendor research)


AI & Machine Learning


OpenRouter drops three AI inference providers after months of prompt theft found by Dragos


Nov 22, 03:14


Dragos researchers found that attackers had stolen data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the providers knew until they were told. Some of the stolen requests were flagged Zero Data Retention. OpenRouter, the gateway that routes requests to a pool of providers, removed the three and revoked ZDR eligibility for 125 endpoints. In its November 22 incident notice it says it notified all potentially affected customers. The notice is OpenRouter's own account, and the Dragos findings are vendor research.


It shows that a 'zero retention' label from a downstream AI provider is not a guarantee, so anything sent through third-party inference routes should be treated as exposed.


Sources: The Hacker News · Cybersecurity News · OpenRouter (vendor notice)


Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini is an open-weights model that runs offline on a 32GB laptop (vendor release)


Nov 21, 19:02


Mira Murati's Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weights multimodal looped-transformer model. It is built to run offline on a 32GB MacBook Pro or a single desktop GPU. VentureBeat says it challenges the cloud-first frontier model approach. A community quantization already runs it in 5.4 GB of memory, and that thread has 489 points on Hacker News. The performance claims come from the vendor and have not been independently benchmarked here.


It is a first-party release that bets on local inference, which matters if you want capable models without sending data to a third-party provider.


Sources: VentureBeat · GitHub (5.4 GB quantization)


UN talks on 'killer robots' end with an agreement only to 'start discussing options'


Nov 21, 21:03


UN diplomats in Geneva spent a largely fruitless week on autonomous weapons rules and left agreeing only to start discussing options. The Red Cross had urged binding rules within a year, and the UN secretary-general and Pope Leo backed that call. The Verge, citing NPR, reports the outcome. It follows Politico's earlier report that the effort was delayed to 2028.


The outcome confirms that no binding international framework for AI-enabled weapons is coming soon, which leaves the rules to national policy and industry norms.


Sources: The Verge


Technology


NYT: AI is uncovering dormant flaws, so tech outages are 'only the beginning'


Nov 21, 20:11


The NYT argues that decades of treating cybersecurity as an afterthought are coming due, as AI exposes long-dormant problems in vulnerable code. It expects more disruptions as a result. This is analysis, not new reporting, and it follows Wired and earlier NYT pieces on the same theme. The Hard Fork podcast also notes that software patches seem to be breaking everything.


The framing is now mainstream, which makes the case for investing in patch testing and rollback plans ahead of the next round of fixes.


Sources: NYT Technology · NYT Hard Fork


Linebender: advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs


Nov 21, 22:17


A post from the Linebender project, which works on Rust GUI tooling, offers advice to people building new Rust GUI toolkits. The Hacker News thread has 197 points and 89 comments. It is a developer perspective piece, not a release.


It is a widely read view on the state of Rust UI development, and it is useful if your team is choosing a GUI approach.


Sources: Linebender · Hacker News


Firmware rollouts at AI-cluster scale: automated safety gates froze a six-day update (opinion)


Nov 21, 23:30


A VentureBeat contributor describes a firmware rollout that had run zone by zone for six days before automation froze it. The share of hosts rebooting uncleanly in one zone had crossed a safety threshold. The piece argues that release pipelines, not hardware speed, can hold back large AI clusters. It is a first-person account and not an incident report.


It is a practical example of staged rollouts with automatic halts, which is the same safeguard the week's patch-related outages argue for.


Sources: VentureBeat


Business & Markets


A tale of two Nvidias: strong earnings, while tech executives lobby for Jensen Huang's return


Nov 21, 22:07


TechCrunch contrasts Nvidia's latest earnings report with tech executives loudly calling for Jensen Huang to come back after his resignation. The NYT separately reports that the company faces an SEC probe into its accounting practices, tied to questions about chip sales in Asia. The summaries give no earnings figures.


The key AI chip supplier is showing strong results while its governance and regulatory problems keep growing, and that mix is hard to price.


Sources: TechCrunch · NYT Business


Toyota, Nissan and Honda to standardize parts to lower costs


Nov 22, 05:04


Car and Driver reports that the three Japanese automakers will standardize parts to cut costs. The Hacker News thread has 676 points and 407 comments. The summary gives no detail on which parts or the expected savings.


Rare cooperation among rivals points to cost pressure across the auto industry, which could change supplier dynamics.


Sources: Car and Driver · Hacker News


Amazon escalates its fight with NYC Council, putting labels on packages blaming the Delivery Protection Act


Nov 21, 22:59


Amazon is now labeling shipments to claim the Council's Delivery Protection Act could add up to $5 to any order. This follows notifications shown earlier in its app and on its website. The act would effectively ban the third-party delivery arrangements Amazon uses. Last-mile firms with warehouses would need a city license and would have to employ their workers directly. The cost claim is Amazon's own.


It is a high-profile test of whether a big platform can use its customer channels to resist labor-model regulation, and other cities will watch the outcome.


Sources: The Verge


Trump signs law formally ending the penny


Nov 22, 00:12


President Trump signed a law on Friday formally putting the penny out of the mint, a year after the Mint stopped striking it. NYT reports the signing. The summary gives no detail on transition rules for cash transactions.


It is a small but concrete change in retail and payment practice, and it takes effect in the law as signed.


Sources: NYT Business

entry.title: Evening — Nov 21, 2026
entry.content:
PulseBrief's Evening Pulse


Sat, Nov 21, 13:00 → Sat, Nov 21, 18:00


Cyber Security


FBI reportedly breached a second time in two months, this time via the NCIC police database


Nov 21, 15:26


BleepingComputer reports that FBI systems have been breached for the second time in two months. This time the target was the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which local, state and federal law enforcement use to share information. The report is described as unconfirmed, and the summary gives no detail on what data was reached or who is responsible. It follows this morning's BBC report of an apparent hack of the FBI's criminal database.


A repeat compromise of a core law-enforcement system points to a persistent problem and not a one-off, and it is a major incident if confirmed.


Sources: BleepingComputer


BADBOX botnet returns with a record 40 billion daily ad requests


Nov 21, 16:17


The BADBOX malware, found preinstalled in a wide range of generic Android TV boxes, is back running large-scale ad fraud after last year's disruptions. BleepingComputer reports that it is generating a record 40 billion ad requests a day. The summary gives no detail on the number of infected devices or how operators rebuilt the network.


The takedowns did not hold. Cheap uncertified Android devices on your networks remain a durable source of botnet capacity.


Sources: BleepingComputer


AI & Machine Learning


Riemann Hypothesis proof gets a Lean formal verification, with MIT hosting the files


Nov 21, 15:36


The Lean community has published a blog post on a Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis. It is the formal check of the AI-assisted claim by Anthropic's Levent Alpöge, which was unverified until now. MIT's Andrew Sutherland hosts the verification files. The Hacker News thread has 650 points and 526 comments. The summaries do not say whether mathematicians outside the project have independently reviewed the formalization.


A machine-checked proof would turn the week's biggest unverified AI-in-mathematics claim into a verified result, so watch for outside review of the formalization.


Sources: Lean community blog · MIT (verification files) · Hacker News


Many Etsy sellers close shops over the site's new AI policy; Etsy says it will revise it


Nov 21, 15:04


NYT reports that numerous longtime Etsy sellers have left the marketplace because they do not want their work used to train AI. Etsy said it would revise its policy. The summary does not give the policy's terms or the number of sellers who left.


Creator backlash over training rights is now costing a platform sellers, and it shows how much consent terms matter for AI data.


Sources: NYT Business


Effort to regulate 'killer robots' delayed to 2028


Nov 21, 17:43


Politico EU reports that international talks on regulating autonomous weapons have been pushed back to 2028. Russia blocked the talks, but other countries also opposed them. The summary gives no detail on which states objected or what was proposed.


There is no binding international framework for AI-enabled weapons in sight, and that leaves the matter to national policy and industry norms.


Sources: Politico EU


Decoder: can Anthropic afford to put safety first as a public company?


Nov 21, 16:00


The Verge's Decoder podcast, with senior AI reporter Hayden Field, looks at Anthropic's Nasdaq debut and the tension between its safety branding and shareholder pressure. It cites compute commitments of roughly $900 billion over the coming years and Anthropic's governance structure. It also asks why OpenAI seems content to let Anthropic list first. This is a discussion and not new reporting.


It frames the main question now facing the lab behind Claude: whether safety positioning survives quarterly growth demands.


Sources: The Verge


Actors license their AI faces to microdrama startups; a roundup of AI agents that live in text messages


Nov 21, 17:00


TechCrunch reports that an actor has licensed his face to a microdrama startup, a practice already popular in China. Experts question the long-term consequences if it spreads to Hollywood. A separate TechCrunch guide lists the most notable AI agents that work through text messages, from general assistants to family, travel and work tools.


Both items show AI moving into likeness licensing and messaging-based agents, areas where the rules are still being written.


Sources: TechCrunch (AI faces) · TechCrunch (text-message agents)


Technology


Wired: the outages are just getting started as AI forces faster patching


Nov 21, 14:00


Wired argues that AI is pushing companies to patch faster because attackers are racing to exploit newly found vulnerabilities, and that this means years of outage chaos. It is analysis, and no cause has been confirmed for this week's outages. It adds to the debate over whether AI-accelerated patching is breaking systems.


It puts the trade-off between patching quickly and patching safely in front of a mainstream audience, so test rollback plans before the next patch cycle.


Sources: Wired


AWS suffered an outage too, and The Register asks why you didn't hear about it


Nov 21, 15:35


The Register's column says AWS was also hit by an outage during this week's disruptions, but it drew little attention. The summary gives no detail on the scope, duration or cause.


It suggests the week's outages are less visible than the headlines imply, which matters if you depend on hyperscaler status reporting.


Sources: The Register


Show HN: Zero C#, C# without a runtime or garbage collector


Nov 21, 16:39


A Show HN project, Zero C#, aims to let developers write C# without the .NET runtime or a garbage collector. The thread has 98 points and 73 comments. It is a hobby-scale project, and the summary gives no benchmarks or maturity details.


It is a developer-tooling signal with decent interest, but it is early and unproven.


Sources: Zero C# · Hacker News


Business & Markets


CrowdStrike reportedly in talks to acquire Zscaler, one of the biggest cybersecurity deals ever


Nov 21, 14:12


Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing two people familiar with the matter, that CrowdStrike is in talks to buy Zscaler. Cybersecurity News relays that the talks are ongoing and could still end without a deal. Neither company has announced anything, and the summary gives no price.


A deal would be a major consolidation of endpoint and cloud security, which would affect vendor choices and contract leverage.


Sources: Cybersecurity News


Musk at DealBook on politics, a potential merger and Ukraine


Nov 21, 14:00


Elon Musk spoke with Andrew Ross Sorkin at the DealBook Summit, covering his politics, a potential merger and Ukraine. The summary does not say which companies a merger would involve or what he said about it. He is chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX.


Any comment on a merger involving Musk's companies is market-moving, so check the full interview for specifics.


Sources: NYT Business


NYT explains how the US economy is tied to AI, and the risk in that


Nov 21, 16:06


In a video explainer, NYT chief economics correspondent Ben Casselman describes how AI has become a huge piece of the US economy and why that could be risky. It comes the day after the S&P 500 fell into correction on AI spending worries. The summary gives no figures.


It explains the exposure behind this week's market slide, which affects funding and valuations across tech.


Sources: NYT Business


Nvidia: new detail on Huang's culture of humiliation and interim CEO Kress's all-hands


Nov 21, 15:31


NYT adds reporting that Jensen Huang's belittling of employees goes back decades and once led to a confidential settlement with an executive who said he was 'terrorized'. A second NYT piece covers what interim CEO Colette Kress told employees at an all-hands meeting after Huang's resignation. She sought to put his indiscretions behind the company. This builds on earlier culture reporting and the SEC and California subpoena scrutiny.


The governance story at the key AI chip supplier is still deepening, and the interim leadership's message shows how it is trying to steady the company.


Sources: NYT Technology (culture) · NYT Technology (Kress)

entry.title: Afternoon — Nov 21, 2026
entry.content:
PulseBrief's Afternoon Pulse


Sat, Nov 21, 07:00 → Sat, Nov 21, 13:00


Cyber Security


CISA adds VMware vCenter, Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver and Apache Roller flaws to its exploited-vulnerabilities list


Nov 21, 09:49


CISA added four flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday, citing evidence of active exploitation. They affect Apache Roller, Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver and Broadcom VMware vCenter, and one carries a CVSS score of 9.8. The vCenter and Expressway entries follow earlier reports of China-linked and PoC-driven exploitation.


A KEV listing sets federal patch deadlines and confirms exploitation, so any of these four products in your estate should move to the front of the queue.


Sources: The Hacker News


GnuPG warns of critical GPGME flaw: a malicious OpenPGP key can expose application data


Nov 21, 09:32


The GnuPG project says a malicious OpenPGP key with an unusually long user ID can trigger a critical memory bug in GPGME, the library most programs use to work with GnuPG. The flaw (CVE-2026-129975) could be used to steal data from affected applications. It affects all software using GPGME before version 2.3.0, and fixed versions are out. The GnuPG announcement was also the subject of a Hacker News thread titled 'RCE in Gnupg' (166 points).


GPGME sits underneath many mail and signing tools, so check which of your applications bundle it and update to 2.3.0 or later.


Sources: The Hacker News · GnuPG announce list


FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database


Nov 21, 11:33


The BBC reports that the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal database. The thread drew 136 points and 70 comments on Hacker News. The summary gives no detail on what data was reached, who is responsible, or how access was gained.


If confirmed, a compromise of a core law-enforcement system is a major incident, and it lands in a week of unexplained outages and the departure of the national cyber director.


Sources: BBC News · Hacker News


Detail emerges on the AI-agent zero-day: MONAI Label flaw gave root on a university server (vendor research)


Nov 21, 12:03


Amazon Threat Intelligence says suspected China-linked attackers used autonomous AI agents to find a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging server. The bug lets an unauthenticated attacker write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup. The attackers gained root on a university server. The findings come from Amazon's own research.


This confirms the exposed product and the exploit class for the first documented case of AI agents finding and exploiting a zero-day, so anyone running MONAI Label has a concrete patch target.


Sources: The Hacker News


AI & Machine Learning


One malicious webpage let researchers hijack Meta Muse and read private chats and memories


Nov 21, 12:53


Researchers showed that a malicious webpage could extract a Muse user's private conversations and stored memories without triggering any approval prompt. The same attack could be extended to reach credentials Muse stores for connected accounts. It was a laboratory demonstration, not an attack on real users.


It is another agent permission failure in Muse, following earlier reports of the assistant leaking users' private data, and it shows the risk of assistants that hold credentials.


Sources: The Hacker News


Signal restricts screenshots by default to keep AI agents out of chats, but admits protection is 'incomplete' (vendor action)


Nov 21, 09:49


Signal will block screenshots by default on iOS 27, where agentic systems are built into the OS, and on Android versions where it can detect an AI assistant trying to read the screen. Signal itself concedes that the protection is 'incomplete'. This is Signal's own announcement.


A major encrypted messenger is openly treating OS-level AI agents as a threat, and its admission of gaps shows how hard that threat is to contain.


Sources: The Hacker News


ChatGPT shrunk down to run on a Super Nintendo


Nov 21, 12:46


The Register reports that a hobbyist version of a ChatGPT-style model has been squeezed onto a Super Nintendo. Don't expect complex, coherent, or always correct answers. It is a novelty project, with no practical use claimed.


It is a light signal of how far model compression can go, though the output quality makes it a curiosity.


Sources: The Register


Technology


NYT analysis: AI-driven outages and attacks fit a historical pattern of innovation causing failure first


Nov 21, 11:02


The NYT argues that if AI is contributing to this week's outages and cyberattacks, it fits history, where new technologies often cause calamitous failures before they improve life. It is analysis rather than new reporting, and no cause for the outages has been confirmed. It lands in the middle of the debate over AI-accelerated patching.


It frames the week's run of outages for a mainstream audience, but it does not establish AI as the cause.


Sources: NYT Technology


NASA's Mars rover and orbiter both suffer glitches


Nov 21, 08:47


The Register reports that NASA's Mars rover and an orbiter have each hit technical problems. The summary gives no detail on the severity, the cause or the impact on missions.


It is a reminder that the week's technical failures are not confined to Earth, though the scale of the problems is unclear.


Sources: The Register


A monitor was cutting one user's download speed by 75%


Nov 21, 11:36


A blog post tracing a slow connection to a display's built-in Ethernet drew 274 points and 129 comments on Hacker News. It describes the monitor as the cause of a 75% drop in download speed. The summary gives no further technical detail.


It is a practical troubleshooting case that is widely read by developers, and it is worth a look if you use docks or displays with built-in networking.


Sources: tymscar blog · Hacker News


Business & Markets


Anthropic's record IPO meets a rocky first full trading day as markets slide on AI spending worries


Nov 21, 11:03


NYT reports that Anthropic broke records with its initial public offering this week, then had a rocky first full day of trading as markets plunged on worries about AI spending. It describes a disconnect between Wall Street and Silicon Valley. This follows the S&P 500 entering correction territory on Friday.


The market is separating the success of one AI listing from doubts about the wider AI buildout, which affects funding and valuations across the sector.


Sources: NYT Business


EU's Costa cuts proposed budget by €44B and plans a Big Tech tax


Nov 21, 11:44


Politico reports that European Council President António Costa has cut the proposed EU budget by €44 billion. Brussels plans a tax on Big Tech to raise billions for the next budget cycle. The summary gives no rate or scope for the tax.


A new EU levy aimed at large technology companies is a regulatory signal, though the design is still unknown.


Sources: Politico EU


Electric truck maker Harbinger raises $240M Series D, backed by a $300M FedEx order and a military contract


Nov 21, 13:00


Harbinger raised $240 million in a Series D round earlier this month, according to The Verge. The company also has a $300 million FedEx order and a new US military contract. It focuses on Class 4-6 delivery vans and box trucks, skipping consumer EVs.


It is a funding round above $50 million that shows capital going to commercial EVs while legacy automakers pull back.


Sources: The Verge


Von der Leyen says Russian threats are 'less and less hybrid' after Denmark thwarts an assassination plot


Nov 21, 12:43


Danish authorities said they thwarted a Russian plan to kill a Ukrainian rapper in September. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that Russian threats are becoming 'less and less hybrid'. The summary gives no detail on how the plot was foiled.


It signals a rising Russian threat in Europe, which affects security posture and risk assessments for companies operating there.


Sources: Politico EU

entry.title: Morning — Nov 21, 2026
entry.content:
PulseBrief's Morning Pulse


Fri, Nov 20, 18:00 → Sat, Nov 21, 07:00


Cyber Security


Amazon: China-linked hackers used open-source AI tool Cairn to find a likely zero-day and attack universities


Nov 20, 18:30


Amazon researchers say a China-linked threat actor used the open-source AI penetration-testing framework Cairn to persistently attack two universities. In one case it likely discovered a zero-day in a medical imaging application and took over a server. Amazon's CISO said the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction. The findings come from Amazon's own research.


Autonomous AI-driven vulnerability discovery and exploitation by a state-linked actor, using a freely available tool, is now documented in the wild, which compresses the time defenders have.


Sources: BleepingComputer · The Record · The Register


Bell Canada says an 'agentic' attacker stole enterprise customer data


Nov 20, 19:51


Bell Canada confirmed that an "agentic" threat actor breached its systems on November 17 and stole enterprise customer data. The data includes information from a system used to order and provision telecommunications circuits. The number of customers affected was not given in the summary.


It is a major carrier's own disclosure of an AI-agent-driven intrusion, and the stolen provisioning data concerns enterprise network circuits.


Sources: BleepingComputer


China-nexus 'Armory Castle' group reportedly had a further vCenter zero-day ready


Nov 20, 22:03


Dark Reading reports that during the last wave of major VMware vCenter security updates, a China-nexus threat group likely already had its next zero-day in hand. This follows Google's finding that a China-linked APT exploited the earlier vCenter authentication bypass from September. The summary gives no technical detail on the new flaw.


Patching the current vCenter fixes may not close the door on this actor, so keep checking vCenter for compromise.


Sources: Dark Reading


F5 now lists six critical BIG-IP flaws in its emergency fixes


Nov 21, 04:13


Cybersecurity News says F5's emergency release covers six critical BIG-IP vulnerabilities, up from the five reported earlier. Remote attackers who can reach a vulnerable service could crash the BIG-IP traffic-handling process without logging in. F5 also warned that code execution may be possible. The flaws affect specific traffic-handling configurations, and no exploitation has been reported. The details come from F5's advisory.


BIG-IP is an edge appliance, and the count has grown, so confirm that every configuration is covered by the patch.


Sources: Cybersecurity News


Visa and Mastercard leak: data is good for phishing, not for draining accounts, researchers say


Nov 20, 22:27


Researchers who reviewed the data leaked from the Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan third-party incidents say it contains no financial details. It does contain plenty of other information that can make phishing lures more convincing. This follows the earlier report that the extortion group N0n leaked data on about 16,000 customers.


It narrows the risk from direct fraud to targeted phishing, though the shared third-party supplier has still not been named.


Sources: The Register


Other incidents: West Virginia Legislature, Nissan repair system, Container Store, WhatsApp patches, Iceland


Nov 20, 18:57


A cyber incident that began Thursday was still ongoing Friday at the West Virginia Legislature, and it has not spread to other government entities. Nissan shut down a system used for repairs a week ago after a hack attempt, which could delay repairs involving vehicle electronics and key fobs. The Container Store said it has restored its website and systems after an incident over the weekend. WhatsApp patched three flaws. One is an Android bug (CVE-2026-23871, CVSS 3.5) that may have been used in scam messages. RÚV also reports a serious cyberattack in Iceland that is thought to be backed by wealthy operators, though the summary gives no detail.


These are smaller or still-developing incidents that show the week's wave of attacks reaching governments, retailers and carmakers.


Sources: The Record (West Virginia) · NYT Business (Nissan) · The Record (Container Store) · The Hacker News (WhatsApp) · Cybersecurity News (WhatsApp) · RÚV (via Hacker News)


AI & Machine Learning


Riemann hypothesis claims multiply: Alpöge's AI-assisted proof, a competing human claim, and Terence Tao weighs in


Nov 20, 18:21


TechCrunch reports that mathematicians are reacting to the AI-assisted claim, and that a competing human solution has also appeared. The Hacker News thread on Levent Alpöge's claimed proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis has passed 2,200 points. A separate post by Alessandro Masullo also claims GRH, and Terence Tao posted a related piece on Navier-Stokes and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. None of the claims has been confirmed independently.


This is the biggest developing AI-in-mathematics story, but it is unverified and may still be walked back.


Sources: TechCrunch · Terence Tao · Hacker News (Masullo announcement)


Thinking Machines publishes 'Inkling 2 Mini' (vendor announcement)


Nov 20, 21:12


Thinking Machines posted an announcement titled "Inkling 2 Mini", which has drawn about 1,100 points and 207 comments on Hacker News. The summary gives no specifications or benchmarks, so what it can do is not yet clear. The post is the company's own.


It is a first-party model release with unusually strong developer attention, so look at the details before the commentary hardens.


Sources: Thinking Machines (vendor) · Hacker News


House chairmen rebuke US companies' use of Chinese open-weight AI models


Nov 20, 21:25


An investigation led by the House Homeland Security Committee is focused on the dangers of US companies using lower-cost open-weight AI models for certain projects. The Record reports the chairmen criticized the practice. It adds to growing congressional scrutiny of China's role in AI.


It signals possible policy pressure on which AI models enterprises can adopt, with open-weight models from China the target.


Sources: The Record


Researcher plants 2 million canary secrets in prompts; AI supply chain leaks them


Nov 20, 21:59


A test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets showed that data entered into AI tools does not stay private. Ars Technica says the researcher planted 2 million canaries and found the AI supply chain exposing secret user data at an alarming rate. The summary does not name which services leaked.


It is an empirical test that supports the concern that sensitive data typed into AI tools can leak downstream.


Sources: Ars Technica


METR updates its AI 'time horizon' graph: exponential gains continue, but judgment tasks lag coding


Nov 20, 19:15


METR, the AI evaluation nonprofit, published an update to its widely cited time-horizon plot. It finds that some AI capabilities are still improving along an exponential trajectory. It also finds that models are not as good at tasks requiring judgment as they are at coding, according to MIT Technology Review.


It is a closely watched independent measure of agent capability, and this update gives a more nuanced view than the headline curve.


Sources: MIT Technology Review


Amazon's split stance on AI shopping bots: AWS embraces bot commerce while the main site enforces bans


Nov 21, 00:41


The Register reports that AWS is promoting bot-based buying while Amazon's retail site continues to enforce bans on bots. The story points to an unresolved conflict over agentic commerce inside one company.


How the largest retailer treats shopping agents will shape the rules for agent-driven commerce.


Sources: The Register


Technology


Google to shut down Google Assistant on smart speakers and retire the Nest app on January 25, 2027


Nov 20, 19:00


Google says the Nest app will be shut down on January 25, 2027, with Nest thermostats, cameras and Nest Protect alarms managed from the Google Home app instead. Devices, camera history and Nest Aware subscriptions will be moved over automatically. Google will also retire Google Assistant on its smart home devices next year. The announcement is Google's own.


It is a hard date for a platform migration affecting a large installed base, and it shows Assistant being retired in favour of Gemini-era products.


Sources: The Verge


PHP 8.6 tightens loose defaults to curb abuse


Nov 21, 00:28


The Register reports that PHP's annual update clamps down on permissive default behaviours to reduce opportunities for attackers. Stricter defaults can break code that relied on the old behaviour.


PHP is still widely deployed, so teams should test their applications against the stricter defaults before upgrading.


Sources: The Register


Microsoft investigates attachment upload failures in New Outlook


Nov 20, 18:01


Microsoft says some Microsoft 365 users cannot upload email attachments in New Outlook. Uploads still work in Outlook on the web and classic Outlook. The issue is tracked in the admin center as EX1561765.


It is a live productivity issue with a workaround, adding to a run of Microsoft service problems this week.


Sources: Cybersecurity News


Nvidia's Vera CPU: a deeper look at its single-SKU strategy


Nov 20, 19:45


The Register looks at Nvidia's effort to build one CPU SKU to serve many uses with its Vera processor. The summary gives few technical details.


Nvidia's moves into CPUs matter for data-center buyers, even as the company faces leadership and legal turmoil.


Sources: The Register


Power for AI: super-hot rock geothermal pitched to end data center energy woes


Nov 20, 19:34


TechCrunch reports that new geothermal startups are betting they can leapfrog today's leaders and deliver terawatts of electricity nearly anywhere. A separate TechCrunch piece asks whether financing can follow chips and data centers into space, since lenders don't want SpaceX launching their collateral into orbit. These are startup claims, not delivered capacity.


Power supply is the binding constraint on the AI buildout, so new sources and unusual financing models are worth tracking.


Sources: TechCrunch (geothermal) · TechCrunch (space chips financing)


Business & Markets


S&P 500 slides into correction as AI worries intensify


Nov 20, 23:47


The S&P 500 ended Friday down more than 10 percent from its recent high, a symbolic measure of souring investor mood, NYT reports. The drop is tied to growing concern about the AI boom, after Anthropic's debut failed to lift tech and Nvidia fell sharply.


A formal market correction driven by AI doubts is the biggest market signal of the week and may affect funding, valuations and AI infrastructure spending.


Sources: NYT Business


Nvidia: SEC reportedly probing its accounting; board was alarmed by Huang's 'lack of candor'


Nov 20, 20:52


NYT reports that Nvidia faces an SEC probe into its accounting practices, after questions arose over its chip sales in Asia. Wired, citing sources, says the board's main issue with Jensen Huang was a "lack of candor" amid allegations of multiple affairs. NYT also reports that companies linked to Alice Huang, the woman at the centre of the scandal, belong to a network of Chinese tech firms and defense contractors that need advanced computing power.


Nvidia's problems are widening from leadership to regulatory and national-security scrutiny at the key AI chip supplier.


Sources: NYT Business (SEC) · Wired · NYT Business (Alice Huang)


Trump threatens 'tremendous tax' on companies that build data centers outside the US


Nov 20, 19:50


Speaking at a press conference on Friday, Trump said US companies will not be allowed to build data centers abroad and promised a "tremendous tax" if they do. NYT notes it was not clear how he would carry out the plan. The threat comes as states and cities are restricting new data center applications at home.


If acted on, it would reshape where AI infrastructure is built, but there is no mechanism yet.


Sources: The Verge · NYT Business


YouTube reportedly set to pay $3 billion to settle school districts' social media addiction claims


Nov 20, 21:43


Bloomberg reports that YouTube has agreed "in principle" to pay $3 billion to settle claims by thousands of school districts that its addictive design harmed kids. The deal would also add new safeguards for teens. The first bellwether trial in the federal multidistrict litigation was due to start in Kentucky in June. The figure comes from unnamed sources.


A $3 billion figure is a benchmark for liability across the platforms named in the wider litigation.


Sources: The Verge


GTA VI took $3.79 billion on day one, which Rockstar calls an entertainment record


Nov 20, 20:35


Rockstar Games says Grand Theft Auto VI earned $3.79 billion in its first day of sales and sold 32.5 million preorder copies. Rockstar calls it the biggest entertainment launch in history. NYT notes that no movie has ever made more than $3 billion at the box office. The figures are Rockstar's own.


It is a record-setting consumer launch that matters for the games industry and consumer spending.


Sources: The Verge · NYT Business


Judge approves $7 billion Roundup settlement


Nov 21, 04:23


A judge approved a $7 billion nationwide class-action settlement over claims that Roundup caused non-Hodgkin lymphoma. NYT says the ruling is expected to end tens of thousands of lawsuits.


It resolves one of the largest mass-tort liabilities and sets a reference point for corporate litigation exposure.


Sources: NYT Business

entry.title: Evening — Nov 20, 2026
entry.content:
PulseBrief's Evening Pulse


Fri, Nov 20, 13:00 → Fri, Nov 20, 18:00


Cyber Security


NSA resumes normal operations after internal network disruptions


Nov 20, 17:06


The NSA is back to normal operations following disruptions to its internal networks, The Record reports. Some facilities remain under "Code Orange" for non-essential employees, meaning delayed openings and supervisor check-ins. The cause and scope of the disruption were not given in the summary, and it lands in a week of unexplained outages across the US.


A disruption inside the NSA's own networks, with no stated cause, adds to a week of outages and the departure of the national cyber director.


Sources: The Record


Transcription firm used by police and prosecutors left customer data exposed online


Nov 20, 16:46


TechCrunch reports, as an exclusive, that a transcription firm used by police, prosecutors and tech giants exposed transcriptions of police interviews and bodycam footage on a cloud server with no password. The exposure came from a simple security lapse. The firm's name, the volume of data and any evidence of access were not given in the summary.


Criminal-justice records sitting on an open server show how a small third-party vendor can expose highly sensitive data for its customers.


Sources: TechCrunch


BYOD ransomware plays audio ransom messages on hospital and university computers


Nov 20, 13:06


Staff at the University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center heard ransom messages from their computers during an October 26 attack. Two weeks later, a recording from Vanderbilt University captured a voice saying "You have been compromised by BYOD." The audio moves the ransom demand out of a private note and into the workplace.


A ransomware group is targeting healthcare and higher education with a new pressure tactic that makes incidents harder to contain quietly.


Sources: Cybersecurity News


Bazuka Android malware framework integrates an LLM to manage victims at scale (vendor research)


Nov 20, 17:58


Dutch mobile security firm ThreatFabric disclosed Bazuka, a previously unknown Android malware framework with large language model integration for victim management and control. It uses fake screen overlays to hide credential theft and device control. ThreatFabric found it in late October during an investigation into an NFC-relay banking Trojan. The findings come from a security vendor's own research.


Criminals are building LLMs into mobile malware to run victims at scale, which raises the bar for banking-fraud defences.


Sources: The Hacker News


Webworm-linked group rebuilds SoftEther VPN as a stealth tool in government networks


Nov 20, 13:40


Hackers modified the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge into a Windows program called NtMonitor VPN internally. It links an external network to a victim's local network and leaves fewer of the traces defenders expect from a normal SoftEther install. Researchers link the tool to Webworm.


Legitimate open-source networking software is being repurposed for persistent access to government networks, and standard detection for it may miss the modified build.


Sources: Cybersecurity News


In Other News: EU sanctions NoName057(16), Norwegian energy cyberattacks, supercomputer hack, Gemini agents hit Epoch AI


Nov 20, 15:56


SecurityWeek's roundup says the EU added the NoName057(16) group to its cyber sanctions list. It also covers the Norwegian energy company attacks, a supercomputer hack, a new Nightmare Eclipse exploit, and malware that targets CACs left in personal computers. It also notes that Gemini agents targeted Epoch AI. A separate SecurityWeek piece collects expert reactions to the major outages and the AI-accelerated patching debate.


This is a quick scan of the smaller developments, including a sanctions action against a hacktivist group, that did not get their own headlines.


Sources: SecurityWeek · SecurityWeek (Feedback Friday)


AI & Machine Learning


Anthropic mathematician claims Riemann hypothesis proof with Claude; unverified


Nov 20, 17:34


Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he has proved the Riemann hypothesis with the help of Claude. The claim is on his own website and has not been independently verified. The Verge reports that Anthropic has not commented or involved itself, though Alpöge says he texted CEO Dario Amodei about it. It follows yesterday's Anthropic research claiming Claude solved two open black hole physics problems.


If it is verified, it would be among the biggest AI-in-mathematics results to date. Until then it is a single-author claim, arriving the day after Anthropic's IPO.


Sources: The Verge


Paper: language models can rewrite their own weights


Nov 20, 17:29


An arXiv paper titled "Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights" reached 301 points and 99 comments on Hacker News. The summary gives no results or methods, so the scope of the claim is not yet clear.


Self-modifying models are a long-standing safety concern, and a paper this widely read is worth a close look before the commentary hardens.


Sources: arXiv · Hacker News


Google workers urge employer not to punish schools that decline AI


Nov 20, 17:59


Google and Alphabet workers are petitioning the company not to penalize schools that don't want Gemini and other AI tools, Mother Jones reports. The story drew 216 points and 157 comments on Hacker News. It is employee activism aimed at a vendor's education strategy.


Internal pushback at a leading AI vendor over how its products are pushed into classrooms points to growing tension over AI adoption.


Sources: Mother Jones · Hacker News


Dutch data watchdog flags safety problems with AI glasses


Nov 20, 17:44


The Dutch data protection authority found that AI glasses can misinterpret medication instructions and other scenarios that affect human safety, The Register reports. The findings go beyond privacy to physical risk. This comes as Meta's Muse Charm wearable is reportedly due in December.


A European regulator is signalling that wearable AI will face safety scrutiny as well as privacy scrutiny.


Sources: The Register


Technology


Linux KVM flaw CVE-2026-99312 let researchers read 127 GB of DigitalOcean host memory from a guest VM


Nov 20, 13:20


Researchers used the flaw to read about 127 GB of a cloud server's memory from inside their own VM on DigitalOcean. On a shared host, that memory can include other customers' VMs. It affects only AMD-processor hosts with nested virtualization enabled, and fixed kernels have shipped.


This is a guest-to-host memory leak on shared cloud infrastructure, so check any AMD hosts with nested virtualization for the kernel fix.


Sources: The Hacker News


Microsoft auto-installs Windows 11 26H2 on unmanaged PCs and suggests a Registry workaround for hotpatch problems


Nov 20, 13:14


Starting this week, Microsoft is automatically upgrading eligible devices not managed by IT to Windows 11 26H2, per BleepingComputer. Separately, The Register reports Microsoft is suggesting a Registry hack for app problems that followed default hotpatching.


Unmanaged and BYOD machines will move to a new Windows version on their own, just as hotpatch side effects are still being worked around.


Sources: BleepingComputer · The Register


AI boom threatens circuit board shortage to rival the pandemic-era chip crunch


Nov 20, 17:01


A trade body warns that automotive, medical and defense orders are being crowded out of circuit board supply by AI demand. Relief is unlikely before mid-2028, The Register reports. It adds to the memory and storage squeeze already in the news this week.


AI buildout is now starving other industries of components, with a lead time that runs into 2028.


Sources: The Register


Software patches are breaking things: outage wave fuels debate on AI-accelerated patching


Nov 20, 13:38


SecurityWeek's Feedback Friday collects experts on whether AI-accelerated patching played a role in the week's major outages. They stress tested rollback plans and the fragility of interconnected systems. NYT's Hard Fork podcast also says software patches "seem to be breaking everything." No cause for the outages has been confirmed.


The tension between patching faster against AI-assisted attackers and patching safely is now a mainstream operations question.


Sources: SecurityWeek · NYT Technology (Hard Fork)


Over 100 Debian packages still ship distrusted CA certificates


Nov 20, 17:39


A scan of a Debian package mirror found more than 100 packages still contain copies of distrusted certificate authority certificates. This was after Debian removed them from the system trust store. Debian developer Steve McIntyre posted the results on the developer mailing list on November 19.


Removing a CA from the system trust store does not protect applications that bundle their own copies, so check what your software actually trusts.


Sources: Cybersecurity News


Business & Markets


California AG subpoenas Nvidia over Huang's China ties and possible investor misleading


Nov 20, 14:21


California Attorney General Rob Bonta subpoenaed Nvidia, saying the conduct of the company and its former CEO "raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors." It follows Jensen Huang's resignation over his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. It adds to the congressional scrutiny of chip approvals and the Gentlemen ransomware claim.


State-level legal action adds a new front for the key AI chip supplier, on top of the stock slide and leadership turmoil.


Sources: TechCrunch


Reports detail Huang's fear-based management style at Nvidia


Nov 20, 14:25


NYT reports that Huang's belittling of employees goes back decades and once led to a confidential settlement with an executive who said he "terrorized" staff. TechCrunch says the reports raise questions about Elon Musk's claim that employees "love" him. NYT's Hard Fork podcast says Huang wants back in at Nvidia.


The culture revelations deepen governance questions at Nvidia and could affect succession as the company deals with a subpoena and a stock down about 40%.


Sources: NYT Technology · TechCrunch · NYT Technology (Hard Fork)


Anthropic's jump didn't lift tech; investors worry about the AI boom and its debt


Nov 20, 14:07


NYT DealBook reports that Anthropic's shares jumped in their debut but did not lift the broader technology sector, as investors worry about the future of the AI boom. A Crunchbase guest column (opinion) compares the AI buildout's growing reliance on debt to the telecom bust. It warns that borrowers' survival will depend on realistic demand forecasts.


The market is separating Anthropic's strong debut from doubts about how the wider AI buildout is financed.


Sources: NYT Business · Crunchbase News (guest opinion)


CFTC lawyers considered probing Trump's memecoin, then dropped it


Nov 20, 16:03


NYT reports that lawyers at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission looked into possible fraud soon after the token's launch. They then decided they would not get the commission's support to pursue it.


It is a data point on how far US crypto enforcement will go when politically connected tokens are involved.


Sources: NYT Business


France and Germany complete political deal on ECB leadership


Nov 20, 17:50


Politico reports that Paris and Berlin have agreed on the ECB leadership arrangement. France's new market-operations portfolio at the bank could become pivotal in a French debt crisis.


Who controls ECB market operations matters for bond-market stability and euro-area financing conditions.


Sources: Politico EU

entry.title: Afternoon — Nov 20, 2026
entry.content:
PulseBrief's Afternoon Pulse


Fri, Nov 20, 07:00 → Fri, Nov 20, 13:00


Cyber Security


F5 ships emergency patches for five critical BIG-IP flaws (vendor advisory)


Nov 20, 11:57


F5 told customers to patch five critical BIG-IP vulnerabilities that attackers can use to trigger denial of service or gain remote code execution. This comes a day after F5's NGINX2Root fixes and public PoCs. No exploitation has been reported yet, and the details come from F5's own advisory.


BIG-IP sits at the network edge of many enterprises, and edge appliances with RCE bugs are prime targets, so this is a patch-now item.


Sources: BleepingComputer


Attackers exploit critical Cisco Expressway flaw (CVE-2026-76466) and reach an internal network


Nov 20, 11:32


The Hacker News reports exploitation of the CVSS 9.8 unauthenticated bug in Cisco Expressway shortly after a public PoC appeared. Attackers breached four devices at a Russian organization and moved into its internal network. The reported victim is a single organization, but the PoC is public, so wider exploitation is likely.


This is another PoC-to-exploitation sequence on an internet-facing collaboration gateway, and anyone running Expressway has little time to patch.


Sources: The Hacker News


N0n extortion group leaks data on about 16,000 Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan customers


Nov 20, 08:35


The leak includes email addresses, phone numbers and, in some cases, JPMorgan Chase account IDs. This explains yesterday's third-party incident confirmations from the three firms, which pointed to outside providers. The leaked set is small relative to the brands involved, and the shared supplier has not been publicly named.


The attribution and data type are now known, and the common third-party link across the three biggest payments names is the real question.


Sources: SecurityWeek · Euronews Business


US national cyber director is stepping down amid unexplained outage wave


Nov 20, 10:14


TechCrunch reports the departure of the US national cyber director. It comes as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages whose causes are still unknown. No successor or reason has been given in the summary.


A leadership gap at the top of federal cyber policy during a week of unexplained outages and major breaches is a notable signal.


Sources: TechCrunch


SonicWall: Gen 6 firewalls will get no more security patches, even for critical flaws (vendor warning)


Nov 20, 11:38


SonicWall urged customers to retire Generation 6 firewalls and stop exposing them on the internet edge. It cites AI-assisted attackers finding and exploiting unsupported edge devices faster. The framing comes from SonicWall, which also benefits from upgrade sales.


Unpatchable internet-facing firewalls are a standing liability, and any remaining Gen 6 units need a replacement plan.


Sources: The Hacker News


European Commission says AI-assisted attack disrupted services but shows no evidence of data breach; staff want answers


Nov 20, 11:51


The Commission took certain services offline to contain the incident, and SecurityWeek reports it has no evidence of a data breach. Separately, cybersecuritynews details the open-source ARTEX framework used in the attack, which hunts for exposed apps, weak passwords and loose permissions instead of zero-days. A union says the Commission has not sent a single update to all staff.


This is a government-scale case of AI-automated intrusion using ordinary misconfigurations, which is the pattern defenders should expect to see more of.


Sources: SecurityWeek · Cybersecurity News (ARTEX) · Politico EU


N-able blames outage on cyberattack; SBC Medical breach grows past 2 million


Nov 20, 10:08


N-able now attributes the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud disruption to a cyberattack that could have led to credential theft. Separately, SecurityWeek reports that the SBC Medical Group breach affects over 2 million people, up from the 1.6 million in the SEC filing. The exposed data is tied to clinics in Japan.


Both are updates to incidents already on the radar, with the provider-compromise risk widening for N-able customers and the healthcare breach count rising.


Sources: SecurityWeek (N-able) · SecurityWeek (SBC Medical)


AI & Machine Learning


Frostbite: a new CPU architecture 'discovered, designed and verified by AI'


Nov 20, 11:01


Architect Labs published a post claiming AI created and verified a new CPU architecture. It reached 510 points and 278 comments on Hacker News. The claim comes from the vendor's own blog, and independent verification has not been reported.


If the claim holds, AI is moving into hardware design and verification, which would be a notable capability shift beyond software.


Sources: Architect Labs (vendor blog)


Signal limits screenshots to keep AI assistants from reading private chats (vendor action)


Nov 20, 10:42


Signal is restricting screenshots on iOS 27 and some Android devices so that built-in assistants like Siri and Gemini cannot read chats through screen capture. On Android the block turns on when Signal detects an assistant trying to read the screen. Signal also published a post on protecting user privacy, which drew 320 points on Hacker News.


It follows the Muse reports that agents can read Signal text via notifications, and shows apps now defending against OS-level assistants.


Sources: Cybersecurity News · Signal (vendor blog)


a16z survey: 60% of CISOs expect to let AI agents act autonomously on low-risk security actions within a year


Nov 20, 13:00


The survey covered CISOs at organizations with more than 1,000 employees. 36% are comfortable with that autonomy today, and AI SOC ranked as the top initiative for 2027. The piece appears in The Hacker News and is framed around vendor and investor interests, so treat it as sentiment, not measured outcomes.


It shows how quickly security teams expect to hand authority to agents, just as agent permission failures like Muse's are surfacing.


Sources: The Hacker News


16-year-old YC dropout builds AI missile startup targeting 'cost per kill'


Nov 20, 08:00


Wired profiles Henrijs Dandzbergs and his startup Polemos, which is developing a missile aimed at making warfare more efficient for the US and allies. The details rest on Wired's profile and the founder's own account.


It marks another sign of venture-backed AI moving into weapons and defence.


Sources: Wired


Meta's Muse assistant can now track and unfollow Instagram users who don't follow back


Nov 20, 13:00


Wired reports that Muse is being used to audit Instagram follower lists and unfollow non-followers, and some people are taking full advantage. It is a consumer feature story, but it shows Muse taking actions on users' accounts. It follows the week's reports of Muse leaking other users' private data.


Agents taking actions inside social accounts widen the permission surface already flagged by Muse's privacy problems.


Sources: Wired


Technology


Palo Alto confirms Java4Shell affects Privilege Threat Analytics, Remote Access Connector and HTML5 Gateway


Nov 20, 11:00


Palo Alto Networks' November 20 advisory says CVE-2026-114938 could let a remote attacker run code without signing in under specific hardware and software conditions. Exploitation attempts began yesterday. Ruby also patched a separate heap overflow, Ruby2Shell (CVE-2026-132825), that could lead to RCE.


The Java4Shell vendor impact list keeps growing while it is under active scanning, so inventory of affected products matters.


Sources: Cybersecurity News · SecurityWeek (Ruby2Shell)


Windows 11 preview update KB5132057 ships 28 changes; optional fix for passkey sign-in error


Nov 20, 10:25


Microsoft's November preview update improves Windows Search, Windows Hello and the Run dialog. The Register reports a related optional update that fixes a bug where Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2 showed a failure message after a successful passkey sign-in on Android. It follows the hotpatch install problems from earlier this week.


Admins should test the preview before it reaches the January cycle, and the passkey fix matters for passwordless rollouts.


Sources: BleepingComputer · The Register


Canonical targets Ubuntu Core Desktop for 28.04, aims to make the immutable OS default in 30.04


Nov 20, 10:29


Canonical's stretch goal is to make the immutable desktop standard in 30.04 without retiring the traditional distro. The plan is a roadmap, not a shipped product.


A move toward immutable desktop Linux from a top distro would change how fleets patch and manage Linux endpoints.


Sources: The Register


ROMULUS ClickFix platform delivers new RAT resembling CNCMachineRMS


Nov 20, 08:11


Blackpoint says ROMULUS appears to work as a delivery service, distributing CNCMachineRMS and Legion Loader through separate chains. It keeps using ClickFix social engineering and signed binary sideloading.


ClickFix keeps evolving into a commodity delivery channel, so user-awareness and execution controls remain relevant.


Sources: The Hacker News


Business & Markets


Bending Spoons to buy Mailchimp from Intuit for €3.35bn


Nov 20, 12:39


The Italian company behind WeTransfer and Vimeo agreed to buy the email marketing platform. Intuit is selling for less than a third of the roughly $12 billion it paid in 2021.


It is a major software M&A deal and a data point on how much SaaS valuations have reset since 2021.


Sources: Euronews Business


Nvidia after Huang: markets weigh whether this CEO exit is different


Nov 20, 11:02


NYT notes that stocks often do well after abrupt CEO exits, but Nvidia's entanglement in US-China relations poses special problems. This follows the stock falling about 40% below its October peak, the Gentlemen ransomware claim and congressional scrutiny of chip approvals.


Nvidia's leadership and geopolitical risk now affect the whole AI infrastructure supply chain.


Sources: NYT Business


China's AI ambitions hit a money problem as US labs raise tens of billions


Nov 20, 11:01


NYT reports that Chinese AI rivals are struggling to match the capital Silicon Valley giants are raising, a gap highlighted by Anthropic's record IPO. A separate NYT video explains how deeply AI is now tied into the US economy and why that could be risky.


The funding gap shapes the competitive balance in AI and how exposed the US economy is to a single sector.


Sources: NYT Business · NYT Business (video)


Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs in Frankfurt and Munich as Iran war slows turnaround


Nov 20, 12:35


Strikes and soaring fuel costs linked to the war are weighing on the airline. Its flagship airline lost an average of €20 million a month from January to September, according to a letter to staff.


It is a concrete example of the Iran conflict's energy shock feeding into corporate cost cutting.


Sources: Euronews Business


EU finance rules to label some oil giants as sustainable, same day EU delays methane rules


Nov 20, 12:38


Politico reports that some oil majors will now be classed as green under EU finance rules. The decision came the same day the EU agreed to delay methane emission rules for fossil fuel companies.


It is a regulatory signal that EU climate finance rules are loosening, with consequences for investors and energy companies.


Sources: Politico EU

entry.title: Morning — Nov 20, 2026
entry.content:
PulseBrief's Morning Pulse


Thu, Nov 19, 18:00 → Fri, Nov 20, 07:00


Cyber Security


VMware vCenter auth-bypass flaw was a zero-day exploited by a China-linked APT since September


Nov 19, 20:21


Google says a China-linked espionage group exploited the critical vCenter authentication bypass before Broadcom shipped a patch, with attacks dating to September 2026. This upgrades the flaw from the CVSS 9.8 patch advisory reported earlier today to confirmed in-the-wild exploitation. The Register separately flags critical KVM and nested-virtualization bugs that hit DigitalOcean.


Confirmed state-backed exploitation of the virtualization control plane means vCenter should be patched immediately and checked for compromise back to September.


Sources: SecurityWeek · BleepingComputer · The Register


Chase, Visa and Mastercard all confirm third-party cyberattacks that may have exposed customer info


Nov 19, 22:12


The JPMorgan third-party breach reported earlier now has company: Visa and Mastercard have also confirmed attacks through outside providers. NYT says Chase reports no sensitive information was taken. The incidents follow a week of outages hitting the same sector, and customer counts remain undisclosed.


Third-party compromise is now hitting the three biggest names in payments at once, which points to a shared supplier or campaign.


Sources: The Register · NYT Business


Gentlemen ransomware gang sets payment deadline for Nvidia


Nov 19, 19:52


The ransomware group that listed Nvidia earlier today has given the chipmaker a deadline to pay or have its data leaked. Nvidia is investigating, and the breach claim and any data volume remain unverified. The listing adds to turmoil that already includes Jensen Huang's exit and a delayed 10-Q.


A confirmed leak at the key AI chip supplier would be a major supply-chain and IP event, and the clock is now running.


Sources: The Register


Second Norwegian energy company breached in two days


Nov 19, 21:14


Dark Reading reports another Norwegian energy company has been breached, coming right after the Equinor attack. No specific link between the two incidents has been drawn.


Two attacks on Nordic energy in 48 hours raise the odds of a coordinated campaign against European energy supply.


Sources: Dark Reading


SBC Medical Group says two incidents exposed data on 1.6 million people


Nov 19, 23:25


In an SEC filing, SBC Medical Group disclosed two cybersecurity incidents that exposed sensitive customer and employee information, including personal data on 1.6 million people. Details on the data types and attackers were limited in the filing.


A large healthcare-adjacent breach disclosed to the SEC adds to the week's run of mass personal-data exposures.


Sources: BleepingComputer


DOJ and DHS launch Threat Disruption Center to take on scams and cybercrime


Nov 19, 18:25


The two departments are partnering on a new unit to triage victim complaints, map cybercriminal networks and give private-sector organizations that work with victims a direct channel. It is a US government coordination move rather than an incident.


It signals a more organized federal approach to disrupting fraud and cybercrime networks, with a private-sector channel.


Sources: The Record


AI & Machine Learning


Anthropic: Claude solves two open problems in black hole physics (vendor research)


Nov 19, 18:30


Anthropic published research saying Claude solved two open problems in black hole physics. The post drew 518 points and 243 comments on Hacker News. The claim comes from Anthropic, and independent expert verification has not yet been reported.


If it holds up, it is a notable first-party capability claim about frontier models doing original scientific work, published on IPO day.


Sources: Anthropic


Meta's Muse agent is mixing up conversations and surfacing other people's private data, report says


Nov 19, 18:38


TechCrunch reports that employees saw Muse surface messages about childcare requests, career advice, product orders and bank account balances that belonged to other users. This lands days after Reuters reported Muse could read Signal text through Android notifications and Mac permissions. Meta's Muse Charm wearable is reportedly priced near $300 and due in December.


Cross-user data leakage in a mass-market agent ahead of a hardware launch is a concrete privacy and security failure mode for agentic assistants.


Sources: TechCrunch · TechCrunch (Muse Charm price)


Apple is hiring to build its own AI agent that can run your Mac


Nov 19, 23:31


A job listing spotted by Bloomberg shows Apple recruiting an engineer to lead an agentic assistant that can browse the web, work across apps, write code and call services. Meta's Muse, ChatGPT and Perplexity can already control a Mac, and Google just added the same ability to Gemini. The listing is a hiring signal, not a product announcement.


Apple entering the computer-use agent race would put an agent into one of the largest consumer device bases.


Sources: The Verge · TechCrunch


Google lets Gemini operate your Mac and puts AI chats on the Search homepage (vendor announcements)


Nov 19, 19:09


Google's Gemini update brings an agent to the Mac that can organize files, fill out forms and run multistep workflows. Google is also rolling out a collapsible sidebar on the desktop homepage to resume AI Mode chats. Both are first-party launches with no independent testing yet.


Computer-use agents are shipping on desktops now, which widens the permission and data-exposure surface highlighted by the Muse reports.


Sources: TechCrunch · The Verge


Lawmakers launch bipartisan AI safety caucus, with 7 of 26 founding members Republican


Nov 19, 22:19


A new congressional AI safety caucus launched amid rising security concerns. The Republican share is notable given the White House's steadfast opposition to regulating AI.


It shows cross-party momentum on AI oversight forming just as Anthropic's IPO raises the political profile of the industry.


Sources: The Record
